No matter if you are the best engineer, or the worst farmer - you will see the exact same benefits under communism. What you have today is what you will have tomorrow is what you will have until the day you die.

Summing up I don't think we should overtly punish those who fail at life. This is why I'm increasingly critical of capitalism. But at the same time we absolutely must reward those who succeed. This is why I'm incredibly critical of communism. I find socialism to be the balance in between.

Mass killings under Communist regimes

Mass killings occurred under some Communist regimes during the twentieth century with an estimated death toll numbering between 85 and 100 million.[1] Scholarship focuses on the causes of mass killings in single societies, though some claims of common causes for mass killings have been made. Some higher estimates of mass killings include not only mass murders or executions that took place during the elimination of political opponents, civil wars, terror campaigns, and land reforms, but also lives lost due to war, famine, disease, and exhaustion in labor camps. There are scholars who believe that government policies and mistakes in management contributed to these calamities, and, based on that conclusion combine all these deaths under the categories "mass killings", democide, politicide, "classicide", or loosely defined genocide. According to these scholars, the total death toll of the mass killings defined in this way amounts to many tens of millions; however, the validity of this approach is questioned by other scholars. As of 2011, academic consensus has not been achieved on causes of large scale killings by states, including by states governed by communists. In particular, the number of comparative studies suggesting causes is limited. The highest death tolls that have been documented in communist states occurred in the Soviet Union under Joseph Stalin, in the People's Republic of China under Mao Zedong, and in Cambodia under the Khmer Rouge. The estimates of the number of non-combatants killed by these three regimes alone range from a low of 21 million to a high of 70 million.[2][dubious – discuss] There have also been killings on a smaller scale in North Korea, Vietnam, and some Eastern European and African countries.

Why should the government be involved at all with something like this? The fairest and simplest solution would be for government to butt out of people's personal lives.

I haven't investigated Bernie Sanders much yet. From what I understand, he is critical of the status quo, which I view as a positive thing, however, as a self described "liberal socialist" and Keynesian economist, economically he represents a philosophy which I believe _is proven to be flawed_.

Keynesian economics is what we have been following for decades and it is at least partially responsible for the current state of our economy. Keynesian economists believe in the manipulation of money, government intervention in the economy, and ultimately a monetary system based on fiat currency and artificial manipulation rather than an economy based on sound money and natural economic cycles. So far this policy has earned us massive inflation, volatile economic bubbles like the 2007 housing bubble, and $17 Trillion in national debt with no sign of slowing down. Why on Earth would Keynesian economics be looked upon as some new policy that is going to save our economy?

Likewise, I believe the philosophy of socialism is also riddled with problems and fallacies. I realize this is a big claim to make without backing it up with a huge analysis so I will acknowledge that we have room to debate on this point, however, in general, I believe capitalist economics is superior because it has a way of establishing an equilibrium, and automatically determining the value of a product or service, whereas by contrast, a socialist philosophy may ignore natural economic principles in favor of state control, not just of wages and prices, but of the entire direction of the economy, which I find less genuine, less representative of the people's desires, less efficient, and less fair in terms of limited ability to incentivize hard-workers.

I can understand how, considering the current state of affairs, someone may be drawn to a differing economic philosophy (and rightfully so!). I think it is important, however, to clarify, the system we have now is not capitalism. What we have is a form of crony capitalism, "corporatism", where the corporations and the government lucratively merge to limit their liability, limit their competition, manipulate the value of products or services, mandate products or services upon the population, direct government spending to certain corporations, bailout certain corporations, and otherwise basically just rip us off. _This is a system where "to big to fail" corporations take advantage of the power of the government to produce an unfair advantage in a way that is antithetical to real capitalism_.
